claims.text: The proposed approach independently computes lattice and electronic thermal conductivity.
The approach combines temperature-dependent ab initio elastic and phonon properties with DFT-derived electron relaxation times.
The approach can predict the thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr within ±20% of experiment from 300 to 1200 K.
Measured total thermal conductivity for an HfNbTaTiZr specimen is 10–17 W/(K·m) from 300 to 1200 K.
Lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are of comparable magnitude below 200 K.
The high-temperature HfNbTaTiZr specimens contain approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Atomic-scale variations in elastic constants and force constants affect phonon scattering.
Oxygen-induced defects modulate elastic constants, force constants, and phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Phonon scattering can be treated independently from electronic relaxation processes in the proposed transport calculation.
Temperature-dependent Debye characteristics modified by defect scattering can represent the lattice contribution.
DFT electronic-structure calculations can provide the electron-scattering treatment needed for the electronic contribution.
Separating phonon and electronic Boltzmann transport captures atomic-scale processes that simpler analytical models conflate.
Earlier models assume defect-free, homogeneous crystals and use single-parameter estimates such as fixed Debye temperatures.
Earlier models misrepresent the balance between lattice and electronic heat transport.
Errors from earlier models can exceed 40–50% relative to experimental data.
The model is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr containing around 1 wt.% oxygen over approximately 100–1200 K.
The model may not apply to substantially different impurity levels or microstructures with high densities of other defects.
The expected improvement is a tentative 20% reduction in prediction error.

contradictions.description: The quantitative improvement is internally ambiguous: reducing a stated 40–50% baseline error by 20% would generally leave an error of roughly 32–40%, not establish the separately claimed ±20% error bound, unless '20% reduction' means an unstated percentage-point reduction.
